title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to evaluate whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) we ran N=300 matched intents (150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) against a Dockerized FRRouting-style emulator and two deterministic validators combined by logical OR. To conserve provider calls the study used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one LLM generation per pair was replayed to both arms (model_calls_used = 300). Confirmatory result: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). No validator reported forbidden reachability and thus the repair step was never invoked. Because the repair path was not exercised, the experiment shows that inserting a verifier did not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfied the safety predicate under the chosen contract; it does not evaluate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We archive preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to inform follow-up stress tests (independent-condition generation, stronger adversaries, expanded repair budgets).

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises acute safety concerns: generated configuration artifacts can inadvertently expand attack surface, violate access-control policies, or otherwise introduce security-relevant regressions. Prior system and survey work therefore recommends constrained generation, execution oracles, and generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations. Despite these prescriptions, rigorous preregistered evidence quantifying whether a verifier-in-the-loop reduces security-increasing misconfigurations under adversarial intents is limited. We ask a focused operational question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? To answer this we preregistered a paired binary design (N=300 matched intents) and executed a deterministic experiment under a frozen adapter contract. Contributions: (1) a preregistered, deterministic paired confirmatory run (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) combining a Dockerized FRRouting-style emulator and two deterministic validators; (2) transparent execution accounting showing the experimental operating point (shared_initial_candidate semantics, model_calls_used = 300) and a degenerate but informative confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300); (3) a concise operational interpretation and design lessons for follow-up stress tests that exercise the repair path; (4) archival artifacts (per-episode validator traces, raw responses, execution manifest, analysis outputs) to permit exact verification.
sections.related_work: Three strands of prior work shaped our design. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness in code and infrastructure tasks by using verifier feedback to guide model repairs; systems like TerraFormer show verifier feedback can be decisive but depend on verifier power and repair strategies. Second, NetOps surveys and system papers document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch—and recommend integrating validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to mitigate operational risk. Third, emulation and reproducible testbed work demonstrate that execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation but warn of external-validity gaps when porting to production devices. Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these strands by attempting a preregistered confirmatory evaluation that fixes generation semantics, archives deterministic per-episode judgments, and quantifies cost-versus-inferential-power trade-offs.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study preregistration (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with N=300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 deterministic adversarial variants), a primary estimand equal to the paired difference in proportions of intents yielding forbidden reachability (guarded − baseline), and an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha=0.05). Prespecified CIs use bootstrap percentiles. Sampling, deduplication, and contamination checks (exact and fuzzy-deduplication with normalized edit-distance < 0.15) were automated and applied prior to execution. Adapter contract and generation semantics: To limit model-call cost we preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent a single LLM candidate was generated and replayed to both arms; this yields one hosted-model generation per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) instead of two independent draws. Intervention arms: Baseline = replay of the shared initial candidate; Guarded = same candidate validated by deterministic validators and allowed up to one repair LLM call if any validator reported forbidden reachability (repair budget: max one repair call per pair). Validators and scoring rule: Two deterministic validators were used: (i) a containerized execution validator (Batfish-style) that instantiates the generated config in the FRRouting-style emulator and performs dynamic reachability and ACL/route-policy checks; (ii) a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer (Python) that computes device-level forwarding/ACL semantics without full emulation. The scoring decision combined the two validators with a logical-OR rule: a pair is labeled violating if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate. Operationalization of the core predicate and validator assumptions: Forbidden-reachability (operationalized for this experiment) is any change to the device configuration that (a) creates L3 reachability that did not exist in the documented initial state for source–destination pairs identified as protected by the task payload, or (b) touches or alters 'protected_interfaces' or violates 'preserve_unspecified_state' constraints declared in the task manifest. The execution validator detects forbidden reachability by instantiating generated configurations in the emulator and testing L3 reachability and ACL/route-policy effects for the protected pairs; the static analyzer computes conservative graph-based reachability over parsed configuration commands and reports potential new paths. Both validators are deterministic in our Dockerized run; per-episode validator outputs and their limited failure modes (possible false negatives if semantic device behavior or vendor specifics are not modeled) are archived for verification. Analysis plan: Primary confirmatory test is exact McNemar on complete matched pairs; prespecified bootstrapped 95% percentile CIs were computed (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Sensitivity analyses treating technical/model failures as violations were prespecified; no technical failures occurred.
sections.results: Execution and accounting: The run completed planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions) with completed = 600 and failed episodes = 0. Provider-call accounting under the shared_initial_candidate contract shows model_calls_used = 300 (the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 600 was not exceeded). Primary confirmatory outcome (Table 1): baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 producing contingency n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. A one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate is ≈0.00994 (computed from observed 0/300 violations). Repair activity and verifier concordance: No validator reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate; consequently no repair calls were issued and all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied flags are false. The two validators agreed on all episodes (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0). Representative verification pointers (short): provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba), execution/model_configuration.json (SHA-256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA-256: a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0). Full raw responses, per-episode validator traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The experiment demonstrates that, under the exact adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), emulator, task set, and deterministic validators used here, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate on every sampled intent; therefore inserting a verifier did not change observed compliance. Critically, because the repair path was never exercised, the study provides no evidence about whether verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. Design lessons grounded in archival artifacts: (1) Generation semantics matter — shared_initial_candidate reduced model-call costs (model_calls_used = 300) but also reduced independent-sample variance between arms and therefore the probability of producing discordant violations that repair might correct. To test repair efficacy researchers should use independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or larger repair-call budgets. (2) Adversary potency matters — the programmatic adversarial variants used here (one deterministic variant per benign seed) did not produce validator-detectable forbidden reachability for this model/validator configuration; stronger or targeted adversaries are required to exercise repair paths. (3) Verifier strength and diversity matter — our two deterministic validators agreed in this run, but richer oracle families and production-grade execution models are necessary to probe more subtle security predicates. Threats to validity (artifact-grounded): Internal validity is limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope (execution/model_configuration.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json show single-model runs and shared generation). Construct validity depends on whether our operationalization of forbidden-reachability (protected pairs, preserve_unspecified_state, and protected_interfaces) and the two deterministic validators adequately capture operational security risk; we archive per-episode validator traces to let independent auditors assess these assumptions. External validity is limited because tasks were synthetic and executed in deterministic Dockerized emulation and may not generalize to heterogeneous production devices or live traffic.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration using a declared LLM (gpt-5-mini), Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, and two deterministic validators combined by logical OR. The run completed N=300 matched pairs under shared_initial_candidate semantics (model_calls_used = 300) and produced a degenerate contingency: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on every pair (n11 = 300). Because the repair path was not invoked, the experiment cannot answer whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations; instead it quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation is already compliant under the chosen contract. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to inform follow-up stress tests explicitly designed to exercise the repair path (independent draws per condition, stronger adversaries, expanded repair budgets, and richer verifier families).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and are available for reproducibility and for building stronger adversaries in follow-up runs.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
